lesson.grammar_point: the unreal past and the subjunctive

listenings.text: Three rules, and I am afraid none of them is comfortable. The first is this. Never answer the strongest version of the argument you were given. Answer the strongest version that exists, even if the person opposite has not thought of it. It costs you nothing and it ends the game where both sides pretend the other is stupid. The second rule is about silence. When somebody finishes, wait. Wait long enough to be slightly uncomfortable, because most people are holding one more sentence back, and it is almost always the honest one. And the third rule is the one nobody believes until they try it. Concede a small point out loud, early, and mean it. It costs you nothing, it buys you the room, and it makes the point you refuse to concede sound like a decision rather than a habit.

The negotiation was expected to take two days and it took nine. What is striking, reading the account now, is that the money was settled by the second afternoon. The sticking point was a single word in the second paragraph, and the two delegations spent eleven hours talking past each other about entirely different questions: one side arguing about what the word would mean in court, the other about what it would mean in the newspapers. Both were right, which is why neither could hear the other. It ended, as these things usually do, with an exchange that nobody had proposed in advance. One side conceded the word. The other conceded the deadline. The agreement has held for fourteen years.

extra_audio.text: Nadia says that of thirty years of negotiating, two sentences did most of the work. He asks whether she meant the first one or said it to buy time. She answers that if you never concede a point, the other side digs in and nothing moves. He admits that conceding feels to him like giving ground on the whole argument. She reveals the second sentence and explains that naming the word turns a quarrel into a problem.
